questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: The language and city - I have lived in Paris (where I went on exchange) during two years (gap years after high school) where I tried to learn better French, developing high school-level French. By going on exchange, the most important factor was for me to improve mig French-skills also in an academic way.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Overall, a very positive experience. Only element of complaint was the bureaucratic inconveniences (but I guess it was expected to a certain extent)

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It came along the way, but I would not say easy. It was easy in the sense that most e-mails were sent with relevant information, however, the system is not very transparent, so you don't get an overview from the beginning, why knowing what you need to do can be a but difficult. Following the information in the e-mails is fairly simple, but knowing it what you have done is sufficient / if you need to do anything else / why you are doing it (what the purpose is and therefore if you are doing it right) is kind of hard to know at first. Key is to be patient and trust the proces I guess.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Not much. You need to seek out the assistance your self. I don't know if it applies everywhere, but as Denmark is fairly developed IT-wise, I think in most other countries the experience is that you have to be present much more in order to find information. In Paris I had to show up everywhere, it was not given that you'd hear back whenever sending an e-mail and calling usually didn't work, as the offices did not speak with one another. However, after showing up they could usually help and they were eager to also, which was nice. (so do yourself a favor and arrive a bit early in order to get stuff cleared out a week before the school starts)

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: We got the information, however pretty late. Also the system of choosing classes/courses was not very well-developed, but I guess it is a part of the cultural exchange to experiences that. In the end it all worked out, just be prepared to adjust to other (less efficient) ways to do things - which of course can be frustrating when you're not exactly sure of how things work. Check your e-mails and seek information by asking on your own - either the offices or other exchange students.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Not very helpful, as I found it through some old friends. However, Cité Universitaire is a place where many people apply (through det Danske Hus), Facebook groups for housing (Danskere I Paris / PadamPadam) or long term rent through AirBnB works well too.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I'd say that I prefer it. Campus is located on the edge of Paris, however trains are fast. I prefer living off campus though, firstly because it is more 'living in Paris' in the sense that you are living among bakeries, restaurants, stores and people so the 'ambiance' might be more Parisian - if that's why you're going. (regrading where, I've lived in many areas over the years, and each arrondissement has its own center, so you don't necessarily have to live in the center geographically in order to get the 'real experience' - if you can even say there is one, each experience will be great!) Living at the Cité is, however, great if you also want to get to know some other exchange students. There will be events and you automatically get to encounter others plus economically it is way smarter! (and still easy to get to school if you go to Panthéon-Assas or Sorbonne)

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I mean, in general, Paris is expensive and so is living, so objectively the housing available is kind of limited and not ideal, but it is what you'd expect in a large city - especially being used to living in Copenhagen (kind of similar).

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: As mentioned above, the system is not very efficient. However, it ended up working out. The thing the most frustrating was getting the pre-approval from KU, as the course catalogue from PA was not published until the week before school. This made things difficult regarding the Online Learning Agreement, as this had been filled out during the summer, and was based on last years course catalogues. The courses being updated/changed and the schedule being fixed (why some classes overlapped and we had to choose new ones) made it necessary to change / modify our online learning agreement, which took some time to coordinate with KU due to case processing time. As we had a deadline for choosing at the host university and had to start following classes, it was quite stressful the first week. However, we managed and it ended up working well.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
1. Course catalogue published the weekend before school started
2. Choosing classes online (all the ones you wished, meaning more than 30 ECTS)
3. The school 'creating' the classes that could be filled out amount-of-student-wise
4. Looking at the final class-proposition and choosing the specific ones you wanted (in relation to this, re-making your Online Learning Agreement, and getting the new classes pre-approved at KU if necessary)
5. E-mailing the host university (and showing up) to let them know, what classes you wished to keep, and which ones of the originally chosen they could delete from your schedule. Now you choose so you only have 30 ECTS and you will be able to participate in the exams. 
6. Getting your schedule on your online-profile (like a KU-user but for PA) and following your classes

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Not much - information from the university, but at first hard to 'understand' their system. Advice is to go with the flow, read your e-mails twice, talk to others, and be patient.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Succesful. I got the ones I wanted and my schedule was great. Good options class-wise and time table-wise.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Choose classes that are CM (cours magistraux) not TD  (travaux dirigé) - if you are taking French classes. The difference is that CM classes are smaller (6 ECTS instead of 10) so you end up having more classes, however, you only have one exam in the end. The TD classes demand more participation throughout the year, mid term test, and presentations. My personal opinion is, that you learn enough French as it is and that the quality of the education is not as good at KU anyway, so no need to be more stressed out through the semester anyway:)

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was fine. Nothing crazy.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level is in general easier I'd say. However, I took French classes as my main goal was to improve my French in an academic way - this made it harder, why I think it was 'lucky' that the content of the classes was not as nuanced as we are used to. (I guess the content is nuanced but as the exams are not pratical cases but more 'apprendre par coeur' (memorizing) the substance/things you need to focus on tends to be less complex)

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Very different. As mentioned above the exams focusses more on memorizing than applying rules. However, the CM classes are only lectures which also made it very different. If you take TD it is also education in classroom like we are used to, so I guess then it'd be more similar.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
FRENCH:
Droit de l'Union Européenne (CM, license, 6 ects)
Droit International Public (CM, license, 6 ects)
Philosophie du Droit (CM, lisence, 6 ects)

ENGLISH:
Cross-border litigation (master, 4 ECTS)
Legal cultures (bachelor, 4 ECTS)
Philosophy of law (bachelor, 4 ECTS)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: It really depends on what your 'goal' is with your exchange. I was glad that I had mixed French and English classes, but the exams will be difficult if you don't know a bit of French already... However, my French is not perfect (based on B-niveau in high school and living abroad for some time)

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Regarding food and personal spendings, it really depends on who you are. I have no idea, as it also changed a lot each month. In general, it's nice to have put a little bit of money on the side (obviously) so you don't feel limited when wanting to experience life - I feel like going out in Paris to eat is a bif part of experiencing their culture, however, it can be done very cheap (compared to CPH) but also very expensive. Really depends.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Basic stuff in the grocery stores can be expensive but at the same time, other things that are expensive at home, can be cheaper (baguette, croissant, fromage - very much what you'd think)

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I think there were a lot, but I never really made that much research in that department.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I bunch I think.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I don't know as I did not participate in any. I know they had a cross country team (running) which one of my French friends did, and I had a Swedish friend who had enrolled in a hiking group - they made trips and everything.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Depends on what you like. Do some research or just walk around in the streets and look around:)

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Easy

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: No - talk to others if you'd like (people are in general very outgoing)

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Non. Pretty much the same as in Denmark. Remember to be more polite towards the teachers when addressing them.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Many aspects - the food, the characteristics of the French people, difficult to pin point

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Be patient, seek information physically (show up), enjoy:)

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: No, I think I've written everything useful.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: New experiences

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Studying in French during the exams - in the end I was a bit exhausted, but you'll have energy for it, as the semester itself is not very challenging (depending on how you structure it ofc)

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
